title: Work as practice
hookLine: a Chan saying tied to Baizhang: a day without work, a day without food
last: FOUR PARTS — ENJOY SOME, BUILD WITH SOME, PROTECT SOME.

lines: AN OLD MAN IN THE FIELDS.
cards: An old Chan master, well past the age for field work, still goes out each day to work the monastery fields with the younger monks. They worry about him, so one day they hide his tools. He doesn't argue.

He just doesn't eat that day. When they ask him why, he answers, so the story goes: a day without work is a day without food. The master is Baizhang, of Tang-dynasty China, and the line has carried his name ever since.

teach.b: In India, by the old monastic rules, monks didn't farm or dig the soil. They walked for alms and lived on what the village gave. When the teaching traveled to China, things changed.
Some monasteries stood in remote mountains, far from any village to feed them, and Chan communities began to farm, cook, haul water and chop wood for themselves.

Tradition credits Baizhang with the first rules for Chan monasteries, built around shared labor. The original text is lost, and some historians think much of the story was told later, but the ideal stuck.
Work wasn't a break from practice. It was practice.
In Japan the same idea is called samu: work done as meditation, sweeping, weeding, scrubbing, in silence and fully. That connects quietly to right livelihood.
Few jobs let you choose every task, but you can choose how you're present for it.
Sweeping a floor with your whole attention and sweeping it while rehearsing an argument are two different afternoons, even if the floor ends up equally clean.
The saying is sometimes taken as a hard rule: no work, no lunch. The story suggests something gentler. Baizhang isn't punishing anyone, not even himself.
For him, working and eating simply belonged together, the way breathing in and breathing out do.

how: In Chan and Zen monasteries, daily work periods are part of the schedule, and residents and retreatants clean, cook and garden in silence as practice; in Japanese temples this is called samu.

games.q: you're an elderly Chan master. your students have hidden your tools so you'll rest. what does the story say you do?
o: scold them and find the tools.
games.why: Baizhang skips his meal and explains: a day without work is a day without food. no scolding, just the two belonging together.

practice: Choose one task you'll do today anyway, the dishes, an email, folding laundry, and picture doing it the Chan way: not faster, not slower, fully, your hands on this plate, this towel.
When the mind runs ahead to the next task, come back to this one, and stay with it here for a while, with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Baizhang. His saying, a day without work is a day without food: in Chan, ordinary labor is part of the path.
